findings.text: Businesses described uncertainty regarding whether their activities fall under the White, Green, Orange or Red category; similar or related activities were reportedly assigned different categories, and some establishments were unsure whether consent was required or whether an intimation would suffice.
The cost of obtaining consent was considered burdensome by some businesses, particularly where substantial fees were payable despite the existing consent remaining valid for a further period.
The technical nature of the application and uncertainty around requirements lead some businesses to rely on consultants or other intermediaries, adding to compliance costs.
Establishments reported uncertainty about the documents, procedures and obligations applicable to their particular industry, especially where category-specific requirements were unclear.

Concerns were raised about inconsistent understanding of pollution categories across businesses and information sources, creating uncertainty regarding applicable consent requirements and compliance obligations.
The renewal process was considered burdensome where the establishment's operations and relevant details had not changed since the previous approval.
Public notices alone may not ensure that affected businesses are aware of changes in categorisation or applicable requirements.
Renewal may require businesses to submit the same documents again even when the establishment's details and operations remain unchanged.
Although the form was not universally considered lengthy, understanding the requirements and selecting the correct service or category could be difficult for first-time users.
Uncertainty remained regarding how far in advance applications should be submitted and when additional charges may apply; the absence of timely, direct reminders was specifically raised.

Some users described visiting the department for assistance and obtaining hard copies or confirmation after online submission, indicating that the online process may not always provide sufficient reassurance or clarity.
The repeated verification of existing records was viewed as avoidable administrative effort when the department already holds the relevant information.

Errors or uncertainty while completing the application require correction or rectification, extending the overall process; unclear industry classification leads to additional enquiries and follow-up with the department.
The discussion included a reported experience of approximately 45 days for obtaining consent; this is an individual experience, not an established average or a verified timeline for all categories.
Provide a clear, searchable classification guide that enables businesses to identify the correct category and determine whether CTO, renewal or intimation is applicable.
Introduce automated reminders through email and SMS before expiry, with clear information on the deadline, renewal requirements and any applicable additional charges.
Simplify renewal by carrying forward existing information and documents, requiring updates only where material changes have occurred.
The experience varied by business type and the respondent's familiarity with the online system; some users reported receiving useful assistance from departmental personnel.

gaps.text: ED states standard CTO processing for Red/Orange categories occurs within 21 days; FGD participants reported an individual experience of approximately 45 days to obtain consent — more than double the ED's stated timeline (though the FGD notes this is a single reported experience, not a verified average across all categories).

ED's fee record describes fees calculated strictly on capital investment slabs with no mention of penalties for early renewal; an FGD participant reported an additional penalty charge was payable despite applying for renewal before the existing consent had expired.

ED records applicantOfficeVisit as 'no' and states the service is '100% online and paperless' with certificates downloaded without visiting the office; FGD participants described needing to visit the department for assistance and to obtain hard copies or confirmation after online submission.

ED's redundant/duplicate-requirements finding states the official reported 'no compliance burden or redundant requirement' in the CTO process; FGD participants directly contradicted this, describing repeated submission of the same documents during renewal and repeated verification of records the department already holds as avoidable administrative effort.

FGD participants reported that similar or related business activities were sometimes assigned different pollution categories (White/Green/Orange/Red) by different information sources, creating uncertainty about whether CTO, renewal, or mere intimation applies — the ED record does not address consistency of category assignment across similar businesses.

findings.text: Participants reported that applicants are not informed when their licence will be issued or renewed; delays affect business operations and the ability to provide valid licences to customers and government departments.
Businesses must maintain physical registers of sales and transactions despite the availability of online records, increasing compliance burden and raising concerns about confidentiality.
The same documents, including identity and business registration proofs, must be submitted during renewals, even when no changes have occurred.
File-size restrictions require documents to be compressed, sometimes making them unreadable and necessitating physical visits to the department.
Annual renewal requirements and repeated fee payments were considered burdensome, with participants recommending longer licence validity.
Participants suggested extending licence validity to five or more years instead of requiring annual renewal.
Different state-level rules, procedures and fees create difficulties for businesses operating across states.
Participants proposed allowing manufacturers to issue verification certificates for their own products, subject to departmental oversight, to reduce duplication and improve efficiency.
Applications are submitted online, but unreadable documents or technical issues sometimes require physical visits and manual submission.
Applicants must repeatedly submit existing documents and maintain prescribed physical registers despite digital records being available.
Delays reportedly depend on departmental scrutiny, staff availability and officer transfers. The Chandigarh Right to Service listing specifies a 30-day timeline for licence issuance and renewal.
Participants reported repeatedly submitting documents such as Aadhaar, PAN and business-related certificates during annual renewals, even when the information remains unchanged.
Physical sales registers were considered duplicative because relevant records are also maintained online.
Absence of a clearly communicated timeline and limited application-status visibility contributes to delay.
Departmental workload, staff transfers and pending scrutiny were cited as reasons for delay.
Remove the requirement for physical registers where equivalent digital records are available and accessible to the department.
Extend licence validity and reduce repetitive renewal formalities; introduce application tracking and clear processing timelines.
Participants considered the online application form relatively simple and stated that third-party agents were generally not necessary.

findings.text: Renewal becomes difficult when the original applicant or authorised person has changed and the previous login credentials are unavailable; one case required a visit to the department to restore access.
Previously submitted fire-safety plans and building-related documents may need to be uploaded again during renewal, even where no material changes have occurred.
Concerns were raised about additional requirements emerging during inspections, including cases where equipment requirements appeared to differ from earlier assessments.
The combined cost of statutory fees, fire-safety equipment and related professional assistance was considered burdensome, particularly for some commercial establishments.

The existing area- and business-based fee calculation was questioned, particularly for establishments that already maintain their own fire-safety infrastructure. The discussion included a reported fee of ₹11 lakh for a large commercial property for a three-year period; this figure has not been independently verified.
The three-year renewal cycle was considered restrictive in cases where the premises, occupancy and fire-safety arrangements remain unchanged.

Differences in fire-safety requirements across locations and in their interpretation by inspecting officers were highlighted as sources of uncertainty, though requirements can legitimately vary by building height, occupancy, use and risk.
Updates to fire-safety standards may not reach establishments directly, leaving them unaware of revised requirements until renewal or inspection.
Renewal follows a largely fresh-application process: existing information and documents are not necessarily carried forward in a way that eliminates repeated data entry and uploads.
The portal's account-access process and document-upload restrictions create difficulties, particularly for applicants managing large files or unfamiliar with the system.
Additional shortcomings may be communicated during or after inspection; the basis for certain requirements was not always perceived as clear or consistent.
A consolidated, easily accessible explanation of the application process, required documents and inspection criteria was not evident to participants during the discussion.
Re-submission of previously approved fire-safety plans and building documents was considered unnecessary where the premises and relevant safety arrangements remain unchanged.
Additional objections or compliance requirements raised during scrutiny and inspection can extend the time needed to obtain renewal.
Differences in interpretation between inspecting officers may lead to further clarification, additional equipment requirements or repeated compliance work.
Introduce a renewal mechanism that pre-fills existing information and carries forward valid documents, requiring applicants to update only changed details.
Provide a standard checklist specifying the documents, equipment and compliance requirements applicable to each category of establishment before inspection.

The online process was described as manageable when the applicant had the required information and documents available; one establishment also reported a positive experience with departmental assistance and inspections.

remarks: This is an FGD-only record and has not been verified against an official ED interview for Fire NOC renewal in Chandigarh.
The concerns raised related primarily to clarity, predictability and consistency of requirements rather than to the necessity of fire-safety measures themselves.

findings.text: Applications may be deemed approved within 24 hours even when departmental objections remain unresolved, raising concerns about document verification.
Establishments with fewer than 20 employees must enter employee details individually, making the process time-consuming.
File-size limits create difficulties when uploading lengthy documents, particularly the Memorandum of Association.
Applicants must re-enter existing information and upload documents again during amendments, even when details remain unchanged.
Participants reported discrepancies in fee deductions, incorrect application routing and inadequate technical support.
Participants recommended reviewing the employee threshold for registration, suggesting a reduction from 20 employees to 5-10 employees.
Concerns were raised regarding deemed approval without proper scrutiny and inconsistent authentication of licences.
Participants supported retaining the one-time registration/intimation approach without unnecessary renewals.
The online process was considered relatively simple, with application completion taking approximately 30-60 minutes, depending on the applicant's familiarity and documentation.
The 24-hour deemed-approval mechanism reduces waiting time, but unresolved objections and verification concerns remain.
Amendment applications require repeated data entry and document uploads, increasing compliance effort.
Incorrect selection of the departmental circle and payment discrepancies require additional follow-ups.
Applicants are required to upload previously submitted documents again during amendments, even when the documents remain unchanged.
Lengthy corporate documents create upload difficulties due to file-size restrictions.
Technical corrections are required when applications are routed to the wrong departmental circle.
Introduce an Excel/PDF upload facility for employee details instead of manual data entry.
Simplify amendments by retaining existing information and requesting only changed details.

The participant-reported statutory fee for registration was approximately ₹2,000-₹5,000, depending on the business category and applicable requirements; this requires confirmation against the current official fee schedule.

gaps.text: ED states establishments with fewer than 20 employees are 'deregulated' and only require intimation/registration, implying a lighter process than full registration for 20+ employee establishments; FGD participants in this same bracket described the same cumbersome, individual employee-data entry process as a specific pain point, suggesting less practical differentiation than the ED record implies.

ED's redundant/duplicate-requirements finding states 'no redundant documentation or overlapping inter-departmental hurdles were reported' by the official; FGD participants directly contradicted this, describing a requirement to re-upload previously submitted documents and re-enter existing information during amendments, which they considered duplicative.

FGD participants described the amendment process in detail (repeated data entry, document re-upload, incorrect departmental-circle routing, payment-reconciliation discrepancies) — the ED record covers initial registration but does not describe the amendment process or its administrative burden.
FGD participants reported discrepancies in fee deductions not being appropriately reflected on the licence; the ED record does not address fee-reconciliation or payment-tracking issues.
